en: The noble, peerless choro
Made ready like a hawk;
To the enraged choro,
Wisdom came from the unseen.
Strength surged from his majesty,
And Sarybai, whom he confronted,
Came straight out to meet him.
When you looked upon the choro’s form,
His mustache swept upward.
When the fickle world was scattered,
He renounced his wife,
Abandoned his people and homeland,
And set out toward the Muslims;
Did he not bring
A great turmoil and calamity?
For the souls left behind,
For the children who would become descendants,
For those apart from his restless soul,
For those destined to remain,
A firm support for troubled souls,
For the children who would remain behind,
Thinking it might one day serve them,
Did not noble, peerless Almambet
Bring grievous hardship
Upon Beijing?
Thinking those here would need it,
Did not noble, peerless Almambet
Bring the blood-avenging Syrbarang
As he went forth lamenting,
And carry it here?
In sport it was Ochogor,
In earnest, a ravenous beast;
When fired with care, it shattered armies,
An attacking foe fell to its bullet,
And in fury it broke whole ranks.
When its report rang out in battle,
In the hour granted by God,
While ill-fated Almambet lived,
It thundered when fired at the foe.
The whole body of mortal man
Shuddered from head to toe.
Where its screaming bullet struck,
The enemy scattered in panic.
When the blessed man bore it,
It was the mirror upon his shoulder;
When it struck a bitterly contending foe,
It was the solace of his entrusted soul.
When noble Almambet died,
Its true place of no return,
To rein in and turn its muzzle,
Against the infidel full of strength,
To charge and level the spear,
He armed himself with all his weapons,
And prepared to meet
His adversary Sarybai.
He appealed to the spirits of Manas, gone to the other world,
Of Almambet and Chubak,
Of Ajybai and Syrgak.
To their spirits he prayed.
“You who pledged yourselves to the twelve holy patrons,
Support me, my mighty fathers!
You who turned from the black faith to the white,
Who fled the infidels and became an exile,
My leopard father Almambet,
Set my undertaking right yourself!
Champion of the Kyrgyz,
He too was one of the precious few;
Foremost among the majestic,
The deftest of swordsmen,
The mightiest of the forty choros,
The leader of them all,
The finest of the forty choros,
Baktagül’s morning star,
The golden canopy of the Kyrgyz,
The warrior of the forty nobles.
Mighty Chubak, gray-maned hero,
We are hard-pressed—support us!”
So saying, Külchoro
Drew his Jazayil and rushed about,
Appealing to the spirits
Of the heroes and ill-fated lions
Who had passed away:
“O sovereign God, I am alone;
Do not let the infidel son of a monster
Bind and overpower my fortune,
Do not, O God, break my spirit.
Do not dig my grave deep,
Do not bend my back,
Do not disgrace me and make me groan.
He is like a saber from Bukhara.
Look at the front of his saddle,
Thick as the Kaldai people.
His beard is like a quiver-case,
And the breath issuing from his mouth
Is like flame from a forge—
Such is his appearance when you behold him.
The hero choro supported by the spirits,
Who rejoiced at the word “battle,”
Whose valor was known among the people,
Whose courage was extraordinary,
Whose strength was manifold,
Whose leonine nature was plain,
Whose nobility was renowned,
Whom no mortal dared confront,
Whom even the surging Flood could not strike—
He had a people numerous as black beetles.
It was his custom to spill the blood
Of all who assailed him.
Though the Chinese swarmed and attacked,
They could not bend and overcome him.
However many mighty giants thronged him,
Not one survived
The noble hero Külchoro.
His nobility became known,
And, saying, “He is famously mighty,”
They inscribed it in the annals
Of seething Khakhan.
His leonine nature revealed,
The gray-maned strongman Külchoro
Donned armor of blue steel,
Slung on his Jazayil,
And prayed to the Creator,
Ready to meet his fate if it had come,
And, if God truly willed it,
To surrender his fly-like soul,
To die if fate had arrived,
And, if God so willed, to behold
The true abode from which none return.
The waterlike ashes of Surat,
“My looming presence at the fore,
My sheltering shadow, Külchoro.
My coat to wear against the cold,
My host of forty thousand warriors.
If I send him ahead, he brings good fortune;
If he follows behind, he is like a countless host.
He rides onward against the foe,
My deep-rooted plane tree at the fore,
Unyielding when he mounts for battle,
My dark-blazed steed, my refuge.
Striking at the shouting foe,
My battle-axe of keen white steel,
My bulwark when I turn to God,
My mighty support on a month-long journey.
My looming presence who takes the fore,
My plane-tree shadow when he rides.
Fire cannot pierce it though tamarisk burns,
An arrow cannot pierce it though fired from a matchlock,
Its collar gold, its sleeves brass,
Double-ringed mail with lark-eye links,
Unwearied when he enters the shooting,
My host of sixty thousand dark-clad warriors.
My cherished Külchoro,
Father, my dear foster-brother,
I turn the mouth of every steed toward you.
From Almighty God,
For you yourself, my valiant one,
I make a special plea”—
So Semetey spoke,
Raising his hands in blessing,
Entrusting him to the spirit
Of Manas, departed to the other world.
He spread his palms and strode forth,
Entrusting Külchoro
To Almighty God:
“May God set this deed aright—
The hero protected by the spirits,
Valiant hero Külchoro,
The courser that races across the desert,
The falcon worth the whole world,
My people who once lived free!
Do not let it be said that Sarybai took them,
Do not break my pride.
Do not destroy my fortune;
Each time we seemed spent, we flared anew,
For we were sons of deep-rooted Manas.
We were servants beloved by God.
Guarding the land and tending the people,
We were sons of gray-maned Manas.
Should a prince’s descendant
Ever fall into misery?
Is it right for a nobleman’s descendant
To suffer such distress?
When Sarybai is his adversary,
Is it right that he should fail?”—
So he cried out in anguish,
Imploring the spirit
Of the magnanimous hero gone to the other world.
To confront the infidel, son of a monster,
To meet him face-to-face,
To sow havoc if he turned,
He urged Surat beneath him,
Throwing the whole world into alarm,
Making him stride high,
Making him gallop with pounding bounds,
Making him pace with sweeping strides.
When your warrior mounted his horse,
Saint Khydyr himself
Seemed to lead it by the bit,
And all appeared as vast as mountains.
From the well-led Kyrgyz people,
What else could the poor warrior do?
He rode out alone from their ranks.
Watching him, Semetey
Shed tears from his eyes,
And his dark eyes, like a merlin’s,
Filled with tears without blinking.
Though he had mustered so many troops and hosts,
His heart smoldered heavily,
And your hero wept, his voice ringing:
“He was a deep-dug defensive trench.
Against the enemy he faced,
He was a host of sixty thousand dark-clad warriors.
He was my shelter and support,
A lion who never grieved.
Almighty God, protect him”—
He spread his palms solemnly,
And cried, “Amen!”
The hero opened his hands in prayer.
Crying loudly, “O God!”
A gray prayer-sash descended from heaven
And settled around his neck.
Turning his face toward the qibla,
He raised his hands, crying, “Almighty!”
And your valiant hero gave his blessing.
Receiving his elder’s blessing,
Külchoro, protected by the spirits,
Set forth toward Sarybai,
Ready to die if fate had come,
To test himself against formidable Sarybai,
The infidel in the fullness of his strength,
The hero of abundant courage,
And meet him face-to-face.
If the true God so willed,
He would surrender his fly-like soul.
He took a deep-blue steel spear,
And donned armor of blue iron,
Buttoning it along his entire body,
The precious armor made by Kanykei,
Wrapping it snugly around his frame.
He pressed onto his head
A helmet no axe could pierce.
Crossing its ties,
He knotted them beneath his throat.
The kandagai worn against bullets
Was such that no bullet could pierce it.
A marksman who could shoot
Anything born into this world
Had been summoned and sent by your mother.
He smoothed the horse’s flanks,
For he was both valiant and leonine,
And all his fortunes were complete.
My looming presence at the fore,
Created by God the Sovereign—
Keep watch over the hero!
Külchoro, my falcon,
Was renowned, and was my support.
